newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE-U.S.-Mexico border becomes fertile new killing ground.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S.-Mexico border becomes fertile new killing ground.

text.p: This Mexican border town across from San Diego, California, once was famous as a playground for drunken sailors and college students.

Today, authorities on both sides of the border warn, it has turned into a gangland run by a growing number of ruthless cartels that sell drugs, run guns and smuggle aliens. Well-organised crime rings also steal cars, rob banks and kidnap for ransom. Along the blood-soaked way, Tijuana has seen a level of violence that local residents compare to Colombia in the 1980s, Chicago in the 1930s or the Old West of 19th century America.

The first to be blamed are the ruthless Arellano Felix brothers -- Benjamin, Javier and Ramon -- who authorities say run a massive drug-smuggling network across 1,000 miles (1,600 km) of border. They have been singled out by U.S. officials as the most bloodthirsty gang south of the border and Mexico has placed a $1 million price on their heads.

"It reminds me of Wyatt Earp and those big gunslingers -- wanted dead or alive," Tijuana Police Chief Jorge Alvarez Barriere told Reuters. "What I don't know (in the Arellano case) is if the reward is for dead or alive."

One favourite Tijuana target appears to be Mexican federal law-enforcement officials, seven of whom have been killed here this year, some sadistically tortured first. Even more state and local officers have died, while two or three revenge killings of small-time drug traffickers turn up every week.

The death toll, along with other high-profile cases like the kidnapping of a Japanese electronics company manager this year and the 1994 assassination of presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio, has sullied Tijuana's once-happy image.
On top of that, the U.S. Border Patrol deports 1,800 illegal Mexican immigrants to Tijuana each day, dumping them at one border crossing.

U.S. and Mexican officials share one explanation for the sudden wave of attacks against authorities -- crooked cops have been replaced with straighter officials who are treading on the traffickers' toes.

Mexican Attorney-General Antonio Lozano Gracia recently named a new chief prosecutor for Tijuana, Cuauhtemoc Herrera Suastegui, who takes over the hot seat as the region's most powerful law-enforcement officer.

Two of Herrera Saustegui's predecessors were assassinated in Tijuana this year, long after they had stepped down as chief prosecutor. And Herrera Suastegui replaces a man who lost two of his top officers last month. Both were tortured and killed in separate incidents in Mexico City.
But Herrera Saustegui told reporters at his first news conference on Oct. 7, "I am not afraid."
Experts said it is too easy to blame the Arellano Felix brothers for all the violence. At least 20 gangs are carving up a limited market, making competition cut-throat.

Three levels of Mexican police -- federal, state and municipal -- have paid the price. But the motives for murder are not always clear, in part because in Tijuana it is hard to tell the cops from the robbers.
Police Chief Alvarez Barriere estimated that 15 percent of the 1,200 officers under his command may be crooked. Many people say that estimate is on the low side.
The string of deaths of federal officials has led to the widespread belief that the victims were in league with organised crime and paid a price for internal squabbling.

"In the 1980s there was a healthy distance between the cartels and the corrupt authorities that allowed for a peaceful atmosphere," said Victor Clark Alfaro, a prominent human rights activist and life-long student of the border. "But in the 1990s this balance has been shattered."

U.S. authorities also have been corrupted, this at a time when U.S. Customs drug-seizure statistics show that Southern California has replaced South Texas and before that Southern Florida as the entry point of choice for drug traffickers.

Three U.S. Customs inspectors from San Diego have been prosecuted on corruption charges in the past three years, said Charles Harrison, a top Customs agent in San Diego. "Obviously these big (drug smuggling) operations can pay (in one bribe) as much as an inspector makes in a year (about $50,000)," Harrison told Reuters.

Still, Clark Alfaro, the human rights activist, disputes comparisons between Tijuana and Al Capone's Chicago or Pablo Escobar's Medellin and instead attributes the violence to the growth of a city approaching a population of two million with problems similar to those of any big city.
"The difference," he said, "is that in New York they don't kill the head of the FBI."
